    Unmasking Accountability: Judging Performance in an Interdependent World

    Abstract

    As local conditions come to reflect extralocal forces, signals of government competence grow more obscure. Yet we know relatively little about how voters evaluate incumbent performance in the context of interdependence. We use a series of simulated voting tasks to examine three theoretical possibilities: blind retrospection, rational discounting, and benchmarking. Across five experiments requiring “voters” to judge performance in a setting that obscures incumbent competence, we find consistent evidence of benchmarking—subjects rewarded incumbents, capable or otherwise, who outperformed a peer. Benchmarking was evident in information processing, information seeking, and both hard and easy tasks. The disposition to benchmark was also generally robust to the availability of information that clarified incumbent competence. Our findings advance the study of performance voting, especially its underlying mechanisms, and raise questions about the availability of performance information across domains of government action.

Unmasking Accountability: Judging Performance
in an Interdependent World
Austin Hart, American University
J. Scott Matthews, Memorial University
As local conditions come to reﬂect extralocal forces, signals of government competence grow more obscure. Yet we know
relatively little about how voters evaluate incumbent performance in the context of interdependence. We use a series of
simulated voting tasks to examine three theoretical possibilities: blind retrospection, rational discounting, and bench-
marking. Across ﬁve experiments requiring “voters” to judge performance in a setting that obscures incumbent com-
petence, we ﬁnd consistent evidence of benchmarking—subjects rewarded incumbents, capable or otherwise, who out-
performed a peer. Benchmarking was evident in information processing, information seeking, and both hard and easy
tasks. The disposition to benchmark was also generally robust to the availability of information that clariﬁed incumbent
competence. Our ﬁndings advance the study of performance voting, especially its underlying mechanisms, and raise ques-
tions about the availability of performance information across domains of government action.
What do changes in the rate of unemployment or
violent crime tell us about government compe-
tence? Students of voting behavior have long as-
sumed that citizens readily attribute responsibility for the state
of things to elected ofﬁcials, and evidence of performance voting
abounds.1 Most notably, a growing economy appears to buoy
the election prospects of incumbent-party candidates (e.g.,
Kramer 1971; Lewis-Beck 1988). However, the challenge of
judging a representative’s stewardship is aggravated by the
growing linkages between individuals, businesses, and govern-
ments around the world. These interactions—globalization in
the broadest sense—yoke local conditions to extralocal forces,
constraining government agency on the one hand and creating
uncertainty about government competence on the other.2 After
all, voters in an interdependent system experience changes in
well-being, but they cannot observe their representatives’ con-
tribution to those changes. How do voters in such contexts as-
sess an incumbent’s performance?
Prior research suggests three competing theories of per-
formance voting under interdependence: blind retrospection,
rational discounting, and benchmarking. Blind retrospection
(e.g., Achen and Bartels 2016) implies that voters ignore the
problem of interdependence altogether. Rather than parse “con-
taminated” streams of performance data, the blindly retrospec-
tive voter takes any recent change in well-being as an indicator of
government competence. By contrast, rational discounting im-
plies that voters judge governments with a high degree of dis-
cernment. These voters extract “competency signals” by ap-
plying a discount factor to observed performance (e.g., Duch
and Stevenson 2008). Where local conditions are sensitive to
extralocal forces, discounting voters struggle to ﬁnd clear signs
of their representatives’ contributions and, thus, learn to credit

the government for only a fraction of observed changes. Finally,
the benchmarking citizen (e.g., Kayser and Peress 2012; Olsen
2017) copes with interdependence by judging performance in
relative terms. Comparative by nature (e.g., Festinger 1954), es-
pecially when evaluating performance (e.g., Simon 1937), these
voters see government competence in the gap between con-
ditions at home and conditions elsewhere. If, for instance, the
economy of a state in a wheat-exporting region is growing at
an annual rate of 4%, while neighboring states are growing at
a rate of 6%, benchmarking voters see the difference—a two-
point contraction—as the government’s contribution to growth.
In sharp contrast, the blindly retrospective voter credits the
government for the full 4% expansion, and rational discounters
credit government for a fraction of the same (0–4 points).
These theories offer competing visions of performance vot-
ing under interdependence and, consequently, the account-
ability function of elections. Paradoxically, existing literature
supplies evidence consistent with each approach, although
largely in observational studies. We seek to clarify our under-
standing of how voters evaluate performance in the context
of interdependent outcomes. Abstracting from the electoral
context, we ask participants in ﬁve experiments to judge the
performance of a factory worker and then “vote” to retain or
replace this “incumbent.” As with a newly elected ofﬁcial, the
incumbent’s competence is unknown and her output varies
over time. In most experiments, the incumbent’s output—
again, like that of elected ofﬁcials—is obscured by external forces;
in our voting tasks, these forces reﬂect the efforts of coworkers,
in a manner analogous to the spillover effect of performance in
neighboring political jurisdictions. The objective in all voting
tasks is to select workers who optimize factory production—a
quantity we link to a material payout to participants.
An experimental design offers a diagnostic test of the micro-
foundations of performance voting. Whereas blind retrospec-
tion, rational discounting, and benchmarking are often in-
distinguishable in observational studies, our simulated voting
tasks allow us to manipulate endogenous and exogenous com-
ponents of performance and to isolate the response to each. This
approach follows recent work on performance evaluation (e.g.,
Olsen 2017). Moreover, abstract or simulated voting tasks like
ours have been used to test speciﬁc predictions of the bench-
marking (e.g., Hansen, Olsen, and Bech 2015) and blind retro-
spection (e.g., Huber, Hill, and Lenz 2012) theories in past re-
search. Further, the alignment between our experimental design
and the actually existing circumstances of performance voting
allows, as we argue below, careful generalization of our ﬁndings
to a range of real-world settings in which accountability-seeking
voters confront the problem of outcome interdependence.
The ﬁrst experiment assesses individuals’ capacity to judge
an incumbent whose performance is obscured by a high- or
low-variance “comparator” (akin to evaluating growth in an
open vs. closed economy). The second tests the ability to eval-
uate an unobscured performance signal without reference to
an irrelevant peer. The third assesses individuals’ ability to
judge performance masked by the efforts of multiple compar-
ators. The ﬁnal two studies examine the relative taste for and
reaction to different performance cues: naive indicators of ag-
gregate performance, decomposed competence indicators, and
benchmarked comparisons.
We report several important ﬁndings. Most importantly,
we ﬁnd consistent evidence of benchmark processing. Rather
than disregard an irrelevant peer’s performance as rational
discounting theory predicts, or overreact to it as blind retro-
spection implies, our participants used comparator perfor-
mance as a baseline against which to judge the incumbent.
Participants in both hard and easy tasks rewarded incumbents—
competent or otherwise—for outperforming their comparators.
We also observe a clear taste for benchmarked indicators of
performance over direct measures of competence. Finally, while
the benchmark response is persistent, we ﬁnd that exposure to
clearly diagnostic information about incumbent performance
may weaken the response in certain contexts.
CONFRONTING INTERDEPENDENCE:
COMPETING APPROACHES
Evaluating government performance in the context of inter-
dependence is a fundamental challenge of representative de-
mocracy, and it confounds voting over a wide range of issues
and across levels of government. Success in reducing a city’s
gun violence, for instance, depends in part on gun control and
law enforcement efforts in other jurisdictions (e.g., Pierce et al.
2004). Voters in such contexts confront the challenge of judg-
ing outcomes driven by the efforts of numerous actors, only
some of whom they are in a position to discipline.3 The failure
to decompose such outcomes in a way that allows voters to
judge incumbents for their part in the process disrupts the
accountability function of elections. In the worst-case scenario,
an above-average incumbent fails to be reelected owing to spill-
over from below-average performance in other jurisdictions.
Prior research suggests three ways in which voters judge
performance for interdependent outcomes: blind retrospection,
rational discounting, and benchmarking. The most concerning
3. Note the distinction between interdependent and collectively pro-
duced outcomes. While both are multiagent processes in which the agents’
individual efforts are unknown to the principal, agents in collectives work
toward a joint outcome (e.g., the parties of a governing coalition ﬁghting un-
employment). Moreover, voters evaluating collectively produced outcomes
typically have the power to discipline every member of the collective. By
contrast, interdependence is the contingency of performance on the efforts
of multiple agents, including agents beyond the voter’s electoral reach.
